# NVIDIA [predictor]{.grad}

Can machine learning beat naive baselines at predicting whether NVDA closes up or
down the next day?

::: {.notice}
**An experiment, not advice.** Nothing on this page is a recommendation to buy or
sell anything. The calls below are published so they can be scored, not so they can
be followed.

## What two decades of history say {.section-title}

Before going live, every baseline and model was tested on past data, always
predicting a day using only the days before it.

{{< include /_generated/backtest.md >}}

::::: {.band .prose}

[How it was done]{.eyebrow}

## Method {.section-title}

### The question

Each day after the close, every predictor makes one call: will the next session
close higher than this one? "Higher" uses the closing price adjusted for dividends
and splits, and a flat day counts as not up.

### The baselines

Three rules that need no learning, and that any model has to beat:

- **Always up.** NVDA has closed up on a little over half of all days, so this is
  right more often than a coin flip. Following it is the same as buying and holding.
- **Persistence.** Tomorrow will do what today did.
- **200-day average rule.** Up when the price is above its average of the last 200
  sessions.

### The models

- **Logistic regression**: a weighted sum of the features.
- **XGBoost**: boosted decision trees, which can pick up thresholds and
  combinations of features.
- **LSTM**: a small neural network that reads the last 20 sessions in order.

Each model's settings were fixed before it was tested and were not adjusted
afterwards to improve the result.

### The features

Twenty numbers describing recent price and volume behaviour, all computed from data
up to that day's close: returns over the last 1 to 21 sessions, how volatile the
last week and month were, two standard momentum indicators (RSI and MACD), how far
the price sits from its 10, 50 and 200-day averages, volume compared with its recent
average, the day's high-to-low range, and the day of the week.

### The test

Testing is walk-forward. A model is trained on the first five years, makes its
calls for the next 21 sessions, is retrained with those sessions added, and so on to
the present. No call is ever made by a model that has seen that day or any day
after it. Automated tests replace all later data with nonsense and check that
earlier calls do not change.

### Costs and simulated returns

The simulated strategy holds the stock on days called up and holds cash on days
called down. Each change of position is charged 5 basis points (0.05%) of the
amount traded. Cash earns nothing in the simulation.

### Limitations

- **One stock, one period.** NVDA rose enormously over the tested years. A rule that
  simply stays invested was always going to be hard to beat here.
- **The backtest flatters.** It is where approaches get compared, so the live log
  is the stronger evidence, and it needs more than a year of calls to say much.
- **Technical features only.** The models see price and volume history, nothing
  about earnings, news or the wider market.
- **Simulated is not real.** No slippage, no taxes, no interest on cash.
- **The data source is unofficial.** Daily prices come from Yahoo Finance and are
  checked before use, but they are not guaranteed.
